10882-the-eagle-s-shadow:
James Branch Cabell published The Eagle's Shadow in 1904, an early novel of society, love, and irony. Its characters include Colonel Thomas Hugonin, late of the Empress of India's service, his daughter Margaret, Frederick R. Woods, founder of Selwoode, Billy Woods, Margaret's former fiance, and Hugh Van Orden, her young adorer. Thirty-three chapters carry their story.

Cabell writes with wit and a touch of fantasy, in the manner that would make his later romances famous. Margaret stands at the center, courted, judged, and gently mocked by the world around her. Readers get Cabell before his fame, already elegant, amused, and romantic.
12192-the-long-shadow:
B. M. Bower published The Long Shadow in 1908, a western novel set on the Montana range, illustrated by Clarence Rowe. Bower, who also wrote as B. M. Sinclair, was a leading writer of ranch romances.

Charming Billy, the hero, faces visitors, fights, canned goods, a man from Michigan, and a dill pickle dispute, while the shadow of an old wrong falls across the range. Chapters move through prune pie and coon-can games, a day of celebration, and Billy hiring a cook, with humor and horse sense throughout. The plot turns on reputation: how a man name follows him, and how he outlives it. Bower westerns are known for authentic ranch detail and easy dialogue.
13543-people-you-know:
George Ade, with pictures by John T. McCutcheon, sketches people who live just around the corner in this 1904 book of fables in slang. His preface warns that no new information is offered, only plain observations in colloquial American language, seldom seen in print, about neighbours the reader may recognise.

A man tries to sell a system of sinking funds, compound interest. New York financiers moved by philanthropy for all persons west of the Alleghenies, until his listener tells him to mosey up an alley. Papa, strung for a month's rent in a progressive jack pot, wakes to cold Welsh rabbits, cigar ashes, and a taste like a lap robe. Ade's humour lies in American types, briskly drawn.
1365-the-complete-poetical-works-of-henr:
Henry Wadsworth Longfellow, America's best-loved poet of the nineteenth century, gathers here in full: "Paul Revere's Ride," "The Song of Hiawatha," "Evangeline," and the lyrics that schoolchildren learned by heart. The poems range from village tales to epics of exile and faith.

Longfellow writes in clear, musical verse, with a storyteller's gift and a moral warmth that made him a household name. The volume gives his whole career in one place. It suits readers who want the classic American poet complete, from first lyrics to last songs. Longfellow's clear, musical verse made him a household name.
13957-the-pocket-george-borrow:
Edward Thomas chose passages from George Borrow for this pocket anthology, from the 1912 Chatto and Windus edition. Thomas notes that readers who know Borrow will dip into him again and again. His selection makes no claim to completeness or authority. Passages run longer than usual in the series, since Borrow is not pithy at his best.

Borrow's gypsies, hedges, and cuckoos fill the pages. A passage compares chals and cuckoos: everybody speaks ill of both, yet everybody is glad of them. Thomas picks scenes of travel, talk, and odd learning. The small volume suits walkers and Borrow fans. It offers an easy entry to a writer best read in pieces.
14201-the-golden-scarecrow:
Hugh Walpole's 1915 story collection follows Hugh Seymour, sent from Ceylon at nine to school in England. As a pale paying guest in houses where other children mattered more, he learned to watch childhood from the edge. The prologue frames nine tales, each named for a child: Henry Fitzgeorge Strether, Ernest Henry, Angelina, Bim Rochester, Nancy Ross, Henry, Barbara Flint, Sarah Trefusis, and Young John Scarlet.

Childhood feeling, not plot, drives each story. Angelina, aged three, broods over sunsets, fountain colors, and spring haze, while her aunts call her morbid and blame a hideous doll for her moods. Barbara, aged seven, knows her dolls bring no happiness and her friend comes less often, yet demands affection fiercely. Walpole writes with sympathy for lonely children and sharp eyes for adults who misread them. The scarecrow of the title watches over a world where grown-ups rarely understand the young.
14402-the-tale-of-old-mr-crow:
Arthur Scott Bailey's 1917 children's book follows Old Mr. Crow, a roving forest bird accused by his neighbors of stealing corn, chickens, and potatoes from Farmer Green. The crow insists he is merely making a living.

Short chapters bring a giant scarecrow, a new umbrella, a race with a train, a game of checkers, and a crow caucus, all told in simple, chatty prose. Jasper Jay and other woodland folk trade jokes and tricks with him. The book belongs to Bailey's bedtime animal series, and it offers young readers gentle mischief without menace.
14701-roof-and-meadow:
Dallas Lore Sharp's nature essays, copyrighted in 1903, watch wild life from two close places: a city roof and the meadow beyond it. Sparrows behind shutters, redwings and marsh wrens by a stream, and a broken rain pipe all become openings for close listening.

Later pieces follow a woodchuck hunt, three sermons from nature, a marsh, kittens named Calico, a sparrow roost, a creature called Mux, Raccoon Creek and a dragon of the swale. Sharp writes as a watcher, not a collector, finding order and surprise in ordinary days. The school edition suits young readers, but its patient attention still rewards any adult who stops to look.
14818-the-daughter-of-anderson-crow:
George Barr McCutcheon's 1907 comedy of small-town detection centres on Anderson Crow, self-styled detective of Tinkletown. Pursuit begins, culprits are chased, an error is rectified, and a babe appears on a doorstep to complicate everything.

Years pass, and the foundling grows into Rosalie, village queen with plans of her own. Elsie Banks, a spelling bee, a Tinkletown sensation, mistaken identity, a disappearance and a haunted house follow. McCutcheon keeps the tone light and the plot busy, poking fun at amateur sleuthing while letting Rosalie steal the story. It is a warm, old-fashioned tale of a village and its most famous daughter.
14916-fairy-tales-every-child-should-kno:
Hamilton Wright Mabie edits this 1905 fairy tale collection for the What Every Child Should Know library, published by Doubleday, Doran for the Parents' Institute. Grimm tales open the book: One Eye, Two Eyes, Three Eyes, the magic mirror, the enchanted stag and Hansel and Grethel.

Arabian Nights tales follow, with Aladdin and the wonderful lamp, Ali Baba and the forty robbers killed by one slave, and the second voyage of Sindbad the sailor. The white cat from Madame d'Aulnoy, the golden goose, the twelve brothers and the fair at later pages complete the set. Mabie's choices shaped a generation's first reading, and the tales still work aloud.
15164-folk-tales-every-child-should-know:
Edited by Hamilton Wright Mabie for the Parents' Institute, this folk tale book gathers stories from many lands for young readers. Tales include why the sea is salt, a lad who went to the north wind, Ananzi and the lion, grateful foxes, and a peasant story of Napoleon by Balzac. Sources range from Dasent to Joel Chandler Harris.

Slavonic tales, Indian tales, and European favorites sit side by side, each retold in clear prose for reading aloud. The book aims to give children a shared stock of world stories. Families today can still use it as a sturdy, wide-ranging fireside collection.
16049-humphrey-bold-a-story-of-the-times:
Herbert Strang's 1909 boys' adventure novel follows Humphrey Bold in the days of Admiral John Benbow. Chapter titles chart his path: the Wyle Cop, a broken apprenticeship, a meeting with the Mohocks, a lost best friend, thieves, a shuttered coach, and a turnpike held at gunpoint. From Shrewsbury streets the tale moves to Bristol and then to sea.

Humphrey takes ship's articles, meets the French captain Duguay-Trouin, fights him, and earns the king's commission, with councils of war and bids for liberty along the way. Strang writes brisk, clean adventure for young readers, full of escapes and sea fights. The book gives a rousing, old-fashioned taste of late seventeenth-century England and its navy.
16247-famous-stories-every-child-should-:
Hamilton Wright Mabie edited Famous Stories Every Child Should Know for Doubleday, Doran and the Parents' Institute in 1907, part of the What Every Child Should Know library. Its contents join Dickens's Child's Dream of a Star, Ruskin's King of the Golden River, Hawthorne's Snow Image and Great Stone Face, Fouque's Undine, and the story of Ruth. Cowper's John Gilpin, Hale's Man Without a Country, Ouida's Nurnberg Stove, and John Brown's Rab and His Friends follow.

Mabie chose tales that teach wonder, courage, and kindness without preaching. The volume served family reading aloud in an age before radio. Modern parents and children will still find a generous, well-chosen treasury.
16507-lazy-thoughts-of-a-lazy-girl-siste:
Jenny Wren, sister of the Idle Fellow, offers lazy thoughts on love, bills, politics, afternoon tea, dress, Christmas, country, town, children and dogs, concerts, dancing, and watering places. The love chapter opens with the poet's line that love is man's side interest but woman's whole existence, which Wren admits with a wink, save for herself as a tenth case.

Wren writes with light, teasing humor, fond of dress and frank about it. The essays are short and chatty, made for an idle hour. Readers who enjoy Victorian light essays will find a playful, self-aware voice, lazy by title but sharp in observation.
16853-fern-s-hollow:
Hesba Stretton, author of Jessica's First Prayer, wrote this tale of Fern's Hollow. Chapters move from a hut in the hollow and a dying father into Stephen's first victory. Threatening clouds, Miss Anne, and a red gravel pit follow. Poor Snip, a gamekeeper, and homelessness appear. A cabin on cinder hill, a rector, and Black Bess come next. An old shaft, a brother's grief, and fire lead to forgiveness and a home restored.

Stretton tells of poor children on the Welsh border, in hills that rise to a broad tableland. Stephen faces loss, work, and wrong with a steady, Christian heart. The tale is earnest and moving, in the style of Victorian children's moral fiction. Young readers get a heartfelt story of home, hardship, and forgiveness, told with warmth.
17088-the-iron-furrow:
George C. Shedd's 1919 novel opens under the Ventisquero Range, tall blue peaks walling a mesa of forest, canyons, and golden sunset light. The iron furrow of the title points to farming and toil on that hard western ground, where a keen-eyed hero watches the land and plans his work. The frontispiece shows eyes under a hat brim, sharp and watchful.

Shedd builds a western tale of land, labor, and love, with desert light and mountain shadow as its frame. The prose is vivid and outdoor, fond of mesa, range, and season. Readers who like westerns rooted in place will enjoy a novel where the country itself is a chief character, and the furrow is both work and fate.
17442-the-guinea-stamp-a-tale-of-modern-:
Annie S. Swan wrote this tale of modern Glasgow, issued in a five-shilling series alongside her other stories of endeavour. The first chapter, called Fatherless, opens in a poor, shabby artist's studio with a latticed window facing north. Tarnished gold frames lean against gaudily papered walls, and the only picture on a worn easel shows a gentle Madonna face with large pleading eyes and a sad, sensitive mouth.

Palette and worn brushes lie scattered where the artist laid them down for ever, and one living creature remains in the room. Readers get a Glasgow story that begins in loss and poverty, in Swan's popular, sentimental manner. The book suits readers of Scottish domestic fiction and of Swan's large following.
17763-the-mystery-of-the-hasty-arrow:
Anna Katharine Green, author of The Chief Legatee and That Affair Next Door, wrote this detective novel with a frontispiece by H. R. Ballinger, published by A. L. Burt Company. Book one, called A Problem of the First Order, opens with cries to let someone speak, a room B, and something to show. A strategic move, three where two should be, and the man in the gallery follow.

Book two introduces Mr. X and carries the inquiry on. Readers get a classic American mystery from the mother of the detective novel, built on deduction and courtroom logic. The book suits readers of early detective fiction and of Green's long career.
17878-bunny-brown-and-his-sister-sue-giv:
Laura Lee Hope wrote Bunny Brown and His Sister Sue Giving a Show, put out in New York by Grosset and Dunlap. Hope also wrote the Bobbsey Twins and Outdoor Girls books, and Bunny Brown was her youngest, liveliest set.

Bunny looks at a skylight and cries, let's give a show, and the children soon plan scenery, songs, and tricks. Chapters bring a climbing boy, a cold little singer, General Washington, and a turn on the farm. The tale is bright, simple fun for small children, with kind adults and plucky young stars who learn to work as a team.
1834-the-case-of-the-pocket-diary-found-:
Grace Isabel Colbron and Augusta Groner's detective tale begins with a pocket diary found in the snow. Its later pages are blurred, as if the writer could not dry them before turning the leaves. Joseph Muller, the modest Austrian secret service detective, must rebuild a life from those damp pages and find the crime behind them.

The story follows Muller through interviews and small discoveries, with the diary itself as the chief witness. Readers who like detection built on documents — handwriting, dates, and the things a diarist leaves unsaid — will enjoy this one. Muller's humility gives the book a tone quite unlike the showier detectives of his day.
18439-what-the-mother-of-a-deaf-child-ou:
John Dutton Wright, founder and principal of the Wright Oral School for the Deaf in New York City, wrote this guide for mothers of deaf children in 1915, published by Frederick A. Stokes. He wrote it at his wife's suggestion, so that mothers might do all in their power for their deaf children.

Chapters move from facing the facts and beginning the work to speech, mental growth, lungs, imagination, and hearing tests. Later chapters take up lip-reading, character, social instinct, schools and methods, and school age, offering plain, practical advice for home teaching in the oral tradition.
18460-flight-from-tomorrow:
H. Beam Piper wrote this complete novelet, Flight from Tomorrow, in which a dictator falls and flees through time. The blurb calls Hradzka hunted and hated in two worlds, dreaming of a monomaniac's glory, stranded in the past with knowledge of the future, yet not knowing the past quite well enough. The story opens the day after a planet shouted Hail Hradzka, when the same crowds scream Death to Hradzka.

Rebels storm the palace, where Hradzka's guards fight to the last among heat-beams and blasters, but Hradzka himself cannot be found. Searchers reach the New Tower, five thousand feet above the palace, blast down steel doors, and climb to a great metal sphere capping the whole structure. Readers get a time travel tale of tyranny undone: a ruler who knew the future, trapped by the past he failed to learn.
18960-the-king-s-men-a-tale-of-to-morrow:
Robert Grant wrote this 1884 tale of tomorrow with John Boyle O'Reilly, J. S. Dale, and John T. Wheelwright. It imagines Britain after a revolution, when King George the Fifth lives in exile in America and a young republic rules in his place. London society, politics, and court life all shift with the change.

Royalists plot to raise the flag again while republican leaders try to hold the new order firm. Love affairs, balls, and court intrigue run beside the political plot. Readers get a witty look at monarchy and self-rule, written as a romance set just past the authors' own time.
1915-the-second-thoughts-of-an-idle-fell:
Jerome K. Jerome, author of Three Men in a Boat and Idle Thoughts of an Idle Fellow, returns with second thoughts. The essays take up love, marriage, vanity, and the small habits of life, written in the same easy, talkative manner. The volume was first printed in August 1898 and reprinted within weeks, a sign of how quickly readers took to it.

Jerome ranges from Hiawatha's fireside, where ghosts are told there is no room for them in this world, to the everyday follies of his own friends. The essays are light but not empty, and they show Jerome's gift for turning an idle hour into a short moral tale, told with a laugh.
19461-tales-of-wonder-every-child-should:
Kate Douglas Wiggin and Nora Archibald Smith edited this set of wonder tales for children, issued in New York in the early nineteen hundreds. It draws on sources from many lands, including tales retold by Joseph Jacobs and William Elliot Griffis, with Indian tales of jackals, Brahmins, and grateful cranes among them.

The stories favor marvels with morals: magic melons that hide treasure, kindly beasts, and truth that wins over cunning. Made for reading aloud, the volume shows what editors of the time thought every child should know, and it still works as a first shelf of world folk tales.
1956-and-even-now:
Max Beerbohm's And Even Now gathers essays written in the years after the First World War, when Beerbohm, living in Italy, looked back on London and on his own youth. The pieces take up theatre, society, and the small manners of a world that was passing.

Beerbohm writes with the same polished wit as in his earlier works, but with a new melancholy: the dandy grown older, watching a younger generation take the stage. The collection is a fine late sample of his art, and its essays on actors, writers, and friends remain models of the familiar essay in English.
19909-good-cheer-stories-every-child-sho:
Good Cheer Stories Every Child Should Know, dated 1915, collects tales of kindness. One opens in the country of the Greedy, ruled by a troubled king. His subjects behave well but love pies and tarts too much. Soup disgusts them as if it were sea water. A policeman could barely make them open their mouths for meat. Such appetites plainly need a story's cure.

Asa Don Dickinson edited this Hamilton Wright Mabie series volume. The Every Child Should Know books stocked home libraries nationwide. Good cheer here means generosity, gratitude, and unselfish joy. Tales from many authors teach those virtues by example. The Greedy country shows the method in miniature. It is wholesome reading, skillfully chosen.
1999-crome-yellow:
Aldous Huxley's Crome Yellow, his first novel, gathers a house party at Crome, a country house modeled on Garsington Manor, where artists, writers, and cranks talk their way through a summer. The hero, Denis Stone, a young poet, watches the party with longing and with irony.

Huxley's chapters move from breakfast to dinner to garden walks, with each guest given a theory of life to defend and to undermine. The novel is a comedy of ideas, light on plot and rich in talk. It announced a writer who would spend his career arguing about art, science, and society through the mouths of his characters.
20193-mary-s-rainbow:
Mary's Rainbow, from 1922, is a children's tale set around a sick child's care. A kindly voice praises Sister Julia and her way with children. One child, now much improved, no longer needs her daily care. So Sister Julia should go to a poor little fellow who does.

That shift of care opens a story of illness, kindness, and hope. Nuns who nursed children play a warm, central role in such tales. A rainbow, as the title hints, promises brightness after a storm. Young readers get a gentle tale of sickness healed by love and skill.
22406-the-little-people-of-the-snow:
The Little People of the Snow is a poem of winter in a mountain glen. It watches a little brook as cold weather transforms its banks. Later flowers give way to white, crystal forms of frost.

Those white flowers grow in clear November nights, the poem says. Later still, drifted snow fills the glen from side to side. A person might walk across the buried stream safely. Many fathoms deep below, the brook still runs unfrozen. It sings to itself and leaps over its pebbles. The poem finds hidden life under winter's still surface. Readers get nature verse that rewards slow, close watching.
22637-a-little-window:
A Little Window is a book of nature poems, written in a loose, singing free verse. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Its title suggests a small opening on a large world, and the sample looks down a gorge at a river in autumn.

The river curls and hums its cadences, slipping past under the gorge's rim as the poet peers through scarlet sumacs. It sparkles in sunlight and shimmers in moonlight, going on and on like a silvery sheet of song. Such verse prizes mood and music over tight form. The collection belongs to the era when American poetry was loosening its meters and turning to the native landscape for its images. It offers a quiet, watery hour of reading.
23277-feats-on-the-fiord-the-third-book-:
Feats on the Fiord is the third book in the Playfellow series, set on the coast of Norway. Its waters are busy with life. Boatmen row out to check the sea-fowl on islet after islet, or carry out nets and rods for the fish that fill those waters.

Sea-trout and char, cod and herrings abound there in their seasons. Between the splash of fish and the dip of oars, the fiord is drawn as a working world, not a backdrop. Readers get children's adventure in a Norwegian fishing landscape, where skill on the water is the real feat.
23300-half-hours-with-the-stars-a-plain-:
Richard A. Proctor wrote this plain guide to the constellations, with twelve maps showing the principal star groups night after night through the year for American students. An introduction and a separate note for each map make the sky easy to learn.

Proctor, author of Half Hours with the Telescope, promises maps true for every year, so a reader can step outside, find the season's stars, and name them. The book made astronomy a home pastime for thousands of American families. One map note tracks the Sea Serpent Hydra at full length, with Alfard the Solitary One near its heart.
23365-in-the-valley-of-the-shadow:
Josephine Daskam set this sombre tale in a large house in October, where Belden paces the library while his wife Clarice lies ill upstairs. A half hour of quick feet, opened windows, and hushed whispers has given way to utter quiet, broken only by his own tread.

Memory fills the wait: a nutting party a year past, when Clarice raced with the children and gathered more nuts than anyone, now set against smells of lavender salts and beef tea. Peter's new step on the stairs brings fresh dread. Daskam writes grief with restraint, through small sights and sounds rather than grand speech, making the house itself feel like a place held between hope and loss.
2350-his-last-bow:
His Last Bow collects the Holmes stories of the years before the First World War, closing with the master detective's farewell to Watson. Arthur Conan Doyle's volume includes The Adventure of Wisteria Lodge and other late cases, ending with Holmes as a spy catching a German agent on the eve of war. The title story bids goodbye to Baker Street.

The collection shows Holmes older, still brilliant, and facing a changed world. Its final pages carry real feeling for longtime readers. For a farewell to the canon, it is fitting and moving.
23766-out-in-the-forty-five-duncan-keith:
Emily Sarah Holt set Out in the Forty-Five in 1745, the year Bonnie Prince Charlie landed to claim the throne held by the Elector of Hanover. The book is written as the diary of the youngest of four sisters, a sensitive young girl whose observations, often religious in nature, follow a Jacobite family through the rising.

Her family, like many Jacobite households, is left more or less alone unless its members actually take up arms. A preacher called Whitefield appears in her pages, and much of the speech runs in broad Lowland Scots. Duncan Keith's vow gives the story its spine: a promise made in dangerous times, and kept at cost.
23942-unborn-tomorrow:
Mack Reynolds's Unborn Tomorrow opens in a detective's office, where Betty looks up from her magazine and tells Simon he is late. Simon, feeling awful and hunting aspirin, says what he needs is a vacation. Betty asks what he will use for money, and suggests Providence turn up a missing jewel deal, a ruby ring down a drain caught in an elbow, worth fifty dollars.

Simon wants five hundred, and Betty wants only her week's salary. Sleuthing, she notes, mostly means snooping around department stores to check clerks knocking down. Then comes a knock, and an old, little man with bug eyes behind pince-nez enters. The title's promise follows: only one thing can be brought back from the wonderful future, and Simon brings it, though he does not want to.
24061-jimmy-crow:
Edith Francis Foster published Jimmy Crow with Dana Estes and Company in Boston, copyrighted 1899 to 1900 and again in April 1902, and dedicated to David. It belongs to a series of instructive books for young children, charming rebus tales for very small children.

Its contents follow How Jack Found Jimmy Crow, The Christmas Candles, and After the Snow Storm. The Rose is Red, Dropping Stitches, and April Fool lead to Jack's Circus Money. Pictures stand in for words in the rebus telling, so that the youngest readers can follow Jack and his crow through the seasons. For collectors of children's books, it is a small, bright example of the rebus tale.
24545-the-tale-of-the-the-muley-cow:
Arthur Scott Bailey wrote this children's animal tale, part of his Sleepy-Time Tales series for children from three to eight years. The series tells amusing tales of four-footed creatures of American woods and fields, with coloured pictures by Harry L. Smith. Its heroine is the Muley Cow, a hornless cow of the farm.

Johnnie Green drives the herd home, and the Muley Cow makes him hunt for her, deciding that hunting for her would do Johnnie good. Bailey's tale is short, gentle, and funny, suited to bedtime reading. Small children get a farmyard story about a wilful cow and the boy who always comes to find her.
24716-the-heart-of-happy-hollow:
Paul Laurence Dunbar wrote this collection of stories, reprinted at New York in 1904 by Dodd, Mead. Its contents include The Scapegoat, One Christmas at Shiloh, The Mission of Mr. Scatters, A Matter of Doctrine, Old Abe's Conversion, The Race Question, and A Defender of the Faith. Dunbar's dialect and spelling are preserved.

His stories portray Black life in Happy Hollow, an Ohio town, with humour, pathos, and dignity. Dunbar, the first Black American poet of national fame, writes with deep knowledge of his people. Readers will find this collection a classic of African American fiction, warm, wise, and beautifully told.
2508-stories-in-light-and-shadow:
Bret Harte's Stories in Light and Shadow gathers late tales that balance humor and darkness, as the title promises. The collection moves between mining camps, coastal towns, and drawing rooms, with Harte's familiar characters facing luck, loss, and unexpected grace. The light and the shadow fall in turn on each story.

The volume shows Harte's mature craft, polished and fond of his old material. Fans will enjoy a varied, satisfying collection. It serves as a good late sample of his art. Harte's late stories mix the humor of his youth with a darker tone.
2524-my-lady-ludlow:
Elizabeth Gaskell frames this story as the memories of an old woman looking back on her youth in a slow English village. Her neighbor Lady Ludlow, proud, kind, and set in the ways of an older age, rules her small world with strong views on rank, learning, and duty.

Through the narrator's eyes we meet French refugees from the Revolution, a clergyman's large family, and villagers caught between old customs and new ideas. Gaskell writes with humor and affection, letting change arrive in coaches, letters, and small acts of kindness. The tale charms as a portrait of a vanishing England and the woman who embodied it.
26313-the-young-farmer-some-things-he-sh:
Thomas F. Hunt's Young Farmer, issued by the Orange Judd Company in 1913, teaches beginners the business of farming. A frontispiece honours R. W. Dunlap of Ohio, who brought alfalfa to his county and raised more wheat from fifty acres with fertilizer than his father had from one hundred fifty. Hunt calls the farmer a co-worker with wind, rain, light, and heat.

Chapters cover essentials of success, acquiring land, farm organization, location, size, and selection. Rotation of crops, equipment, profit estimates, grain and hay, costs, intensive farming, and animal husbandry follow. Later parts treat labour, shipping, marketing, and laws on land and labour. The book suits a young man weighing whether country life can pay.
26934-shawn-of-skarrow:
James Tandy Ellis's 1911 novel follows Shawn, a country boy whose life turns on fishing, friends, and the long pull toward school. The illustrations catch him with his dog Coaly, taking out shells, crossing by ferry, and facing a judge, small scenes that set the tone of a rural boyhood.

Shawn drifts between mischief and good advice, with neighbors like Mrs. Alden urging him back to his lessons and old hands offering rough wisdom in dialect speech. The novel reads as a warm Kentucky boy's book: funny, plainspoken, and built on the belief that a boy can be steered right without losing his spirit.
3481-the-life-of-george-borrow:
Herbert Jenkins writes the life of George Borrow from unpublished official papers, Borrow's own works, and his letters. The biography gives special weight to seven rich years in Spain, which Borrow himself called the five happiest years of his life. Those years had been hard to document, since letters Borrow wrote to the Bible Society were mislaid and only came to light after an earlier life by Dr Knapp.

Jenkins also searched the Public Record Office for fresh material on Borrow's work as a Bible agent and traveler. The result is a fuller portrait of a restless, gifted man who wrote about gypsies, Spain, and Wales. Readers interested in Victorian travelers and in the making of a literary life will find a solid, well sourced biography.
3540-the-census-in-moscow:
Leo Tolstoy writes this short piece from his larger work What to Do, focused on the Moscow census of 1882. He explains that a census is a sociological inquiry, and that the science of sociology aims at the happiness of the people. Unlike other sciences, it is not done by learned men in cabinets and laboratories, but by two thousand young volunteers who visit real homes.

Tolstoy argues that counting the poor is not the same as helping them. A statistician may feel calm about figures for beggars and neglected children, while a visitor who sees their rooms cannot stay indifferent. The piece suits readers who want Tolstoy's social thought in brief form, before turning to the full What to Do.
3541-what-to-do-thoughts-evoked-by-the-c:
Leo Tolstoy writes this essay after moving to Moscow in 1881 and meeting city poverty for the first time. He knew rural poverty well, but the beggars, prostitutes, and uncared for children of the capital shocked him. Taking part in the Moscow census, he saw how statisticians could count people with calm pride while doing nothing for them.

Tolstoy asks what a rich man should actually do, rather than merely feel pity or give small coins. He argues that the division between rich and poor rests on how the rich live and work. The book, translated by Isabel Hapgood in 1887, suits readers who want Tolstoy as a social prophet, turning a census into a moral challenge.
3609-to-morrow:
Victoria Cross, the pen name of Annie Sophie Cory, writes a novel whose title asks when tomorrow ever comes. The book opens with a rejected letter crushed in the narrator's hand and with a feeling of power that inflames every vein and fills the brain. An epigraph from Martial asks Postumus, who always says he will live tomorrow, when that tomorrow will arrive and what it would cost to buy.

The story follows a gifted, restless figure who keeps postponing life, love, and work to a future that never arrives. Cross writes with the passionate, frank style that made her popular in Edwardian England. The novel suits readers who enjoy stories of talent, delay, and the price of waiting for a better day.
3630-what-to-do-thoughts-evoked-by-the-c:
Leo Tolstoy writes this full work after taking part in the Moscow census of 1882 and meeting city poverty face to face. He knew rural poverty well, but the beggars and neglected children of the capital shocked him, and he asked what a rich man should actually do. The book moves from the census to longer essays on science, art, and the division of labor.

Tolstoy argues that the rich live by the toil of others and then excuse themselves with theories of progress. He calls on readers to change how they live, not merely to give alms. Translated by Isabel Hapgood in 1887, the book suits readers who want Tolstoy as a social prophet, turning a count of the poor into a demand for a new life.
3713-aaron-trow:
Anthony Trollope sets this grim tale on Bermuda, a colony he refuses to call the Fortunate Isles. The islands, ringed by reefs and hard to enter or leave, hold a convict station, and from it breaks Aaron Trow, a desperate man with a taste for terror. He forces his way into a settler household by night and holds a young woman at his mercy, demanding drink and company while her family waits in dread.

The story turns on nerve and endurance, as the captive keeps her head and plays for time against a brute who loves the sound of his own threats. Trollope draws the vexed Bermoothes with a traveler's eye and a moralist's frown. Readers who like taut suspense will find a short tale that wastes no words and spares no tension.
3798-reminiscences-of-captain-gronow:
Captain Rees Howell Gronow, a soldier of the Regency and the French wars, sets down his memories as a string of titled anecdotes rather than a formal life. The editor warns that spelling is creative and punctuation varied, with French phrases scattered through, and that topics follow one another with little order beyond the captain's own fancy. The charm lies in that looseness, since each piece stands as a table tale.

Waterloo supplies the finest passage, as Wellington's Guards rise from the ridge at the order to charge, after hours of defensive fire and loss. Gronow writes as a man who was there and likes to tell it. Readers who enjoy Regency gossip, duels, and battlefields will find a book to dip into, with a new story on nearly every page.
41-the-legend-of-sleepy-hollow:
Washington Irving sets a ghost story in a drowsy Hudson Valley village. The Legend of Sleepy Hollow follows schoolmaster Ichabod Crane, who courts Katrina Van Tassel and fears the local phantom. The tale is framed as papers left by Diedrich Knickerbocker.

Ichabod rivals the rough Brom Bones for Katrina's hand and her father's farm. On a dark ride home, a headless rider chases him across a bridge. Irving leaves the ending open: flight, prank, or true haunting. The Horseman became an American Halloween icon. Retellings in film, stage, and print have kept the Hollow's rider galloping for two centuries.
4214-the-puritan-widow:
An early English comedy, The Puritan Widow, turns on players, a corporal, and a household in turmoil. Players are mightily blamed, Pye reports, because they once brought a man drunk upon the stage, and the corporal cannot blame them for it.

Talk turns to an old knight raging over a lost chain, and to a kinsman in prison of such exquisite art that even the devil seems French beside him. The play mixes farce, disguise, and city trickery in the manner of the age. Readers who enjoy Shakespeare-era comedy will find a lively, rough-edged piece.
4265-heroes-every-child-should-know:
Hamilton Wright Mabie edited this collection of hero tales for young readers. He drew on older retellings and poems for the stories. Its chapters run from Perseus and Hercules to Daniel and David. They run from St. George through King Arthur and Sir Galahad. Siegfried, Roland, and King Alfred follow.

Each story is adapted from a known source. Charles Kingsley and Alfred Tennyson are among them. Histories of Charlemagne and the peers of France supply others. Mabie meant the book as an introduction to the heroic imagination. Brave deeds, loyalty, and endurance are told plainly, so children can meet great figures in one volume.
4588-the-allen-house-or-twenty-years-ago:
T. S. Arthur published The Allen House, or Twenty Years Ago and Now, at Philadelphia in 1860, as a moral tale about two ways through life. His preface asks young men and maidens, still lingering in soft green meadows, to choose soberly. One road leads to honour, success, and happiness. The other ends in ruined hopes. Few who start wrong, he warns, ever find the right way again.

The story opens in rain, with a tired narrator coming home wet and weary, and it measures the present against choices made twenty years before. Through one household, Arthur shows how small habits harden into a life, for good or ill. Readers get a short, earnest Victorian lesson in conduct, written to be read by families, and a clear example of the improving fiction that filled American parlours in its day.
460-the-dawn-of-a-to-morrow:
Frances Hodgson Burnett sets this short tale in a thick London fog, where a weary man wakes to gloom and despair. Two ways of seeing the fog open the book: as horror, or as a warm, enclosing mystery. The hero, sick and hopeless, meets a poor woman whose faith and kindness slowly turn his mind toward life.

Burnett writes with soft, vivid detail, from coal fires to foggy streets. The dawn of the title is inward: a new will to live. The book reads as a gentle sermon on hope, where small human care proves stronger than gloom.
4614-from-a-college-window:
Arthur Christopher Benson published From a College Window in 1906, gathering twelve essays first printed in the Cornhill Magazine, with six further papers on kindred subjects. His contents run from the point of view, growing older, books, sociabilities, and conversation. They go on to beauty, art, egotism, and education, then to authorship, the criticism of others, priest, ambition, the simple life, games, spiritualism, habits, and religion. The opening essay argues that personality gives value to art.

No amount of labour, zest, or accomplishment, Benson says, can make up for the absence of that subtle, evasive quality in a book, picture, or piece of music. The essays that follow test that claim across reading, friendship, and college life. Readers get a reflective, civilised volume, written from inside Cambridge, for anyone who likes quiet essays on books, character, and the art of living well.
4916-undertow:
A young couple's marriage plans open this novel, as Nancy's and Bert's families weigh whether the union is a grave chance or a sensible match. Nancy is beautiful and of gentle folk. She insists she is practical and has worked for years. Her Boston mother and his Southern uncle view the match from opposite ends of American life.

The story follows the couple through the undertow of family expectation, money, and class feeling that pulls at a new marriage. The record names no author, so the tale must speak for itself. Readers get a domestic novel about love tested less by villains than by the quiet pressures of kin and custom.
494-to-morrow:
Joseph Conrad sets this short tale in the seaport of Colebrook, where Captain Hagberd waits for a son who will never return. Hagberd, who bought twin cottages and lets one to blind boat-builder Carvil, talks endlessly of his boy's homecoming tomorrow. Bessie Carvil, his tenant's daughter, tends him with quiet pity.

Conrad writes with grave irony, as hope hardens into delusion and a kind girl pays its price. The sea, the fence, and the washing lines ground the sad comedy. The tale endures as a study of waiting, self-deceit, and love that arrives too late to save anyone.
4979-blacky-the-crow:
Thornton W. Burgess's Blacky the Crow opens with a sharp-eyed bird who watches for things not meant for his eyes, and gets into trouble he could easily avoid. Like his cousin Sammy Jay, Blacky sees a great deal he has no business seeing, and winter makes the habit costly.

Snow covers the Green Meadows and Green Forest, ice binds the Big River and Smiling Pool, and Blacky must use his eyes for all they are worth to find food. Burgess turns each scrape into a small lesson about curiosity and caution. Young readers get an animal tale that teaches woodland ways through one crow's misadventures.
5121-dark-hollow:
Anna Katharine Green's mystery opens with a woman in purple. A missing man named Bela may be living or dead, and nobody can settle which. From that puzzle, the story moves through veiled meetings, a house with a secret room, a courtroom. A door of mystery opens, as old family misfortunes come back to accuse the living.

Green, a pioneer of the American detective novel, builds suspense through documents, testimony, and slow revelation rather than chases. Readers who enjoy classic mysteries of manners will find a carefully plotted puzzle, with a strong sense of place and a heroine caught between loyalty and truth.
5231-the-way-we-live-now:
Anthony Trollope's great satire, published in monthly parts from 1874 to 1875. It takes aim at the speculation and fraud of its age. Its central figure is Augustus Melmotte, a financier of mysterious wealth who dazzles London society, promotes grand schemes. He seeks a place in Parliament, while families scheme for marriages and money around him.

Trollope follows dozens of characters, from aristocrats to clerks, showing how greed corrupts love, politics, and business alike. The novel stands as his longest and most ambitious work. It remains a brilliant portrait of a society learning to live on credit, rumour, and show.
532-at-the-foot-of-the-rainbow:
Gene Stratton-Porter sets this Wabash tale among rat catchers, coons, and a rainbow's promise. Dannie and Jimmy Malone, friends and rivals, trap, fish, and court Mary Malone through seasons of rain and sun. A kingfisher, a black bass, and a pot of gold at the rainbow's foot thread the chapters.

Stratton-Porter writes nature with loving care, from river banks to orchards. A life sketch of the author fronts the book, praising her Limberlost work. The novel reads as a gentle romance of country folk, where love, work, and the land itself point toward hope.
5349-castle-craneycrow:
George Barr McCutcheon's Castle Craneycrow, published in New York in 1902, opens with Philip Quentin lecturing his servant on mind over matter. He then cheerfully takes him by the throat and throws him into a far corner. The servant, half his master's size, answers with picturesque language, but his loyalty and faithfulness are beyond doubt.

Quentin's career, already colourful, carries him toward a castle, a mystery. Romance follows, in the Ruritanian manner McCutcheon made famous. Readers get a brisk adventure of the period, with a strong hero, a loyal servant. A plot moves from a servant's scolding to a castle's secrets.
591-flame-and-shadow:
Sara Teasdale gathers lyrics of love, place, and war in this volume, arranged in twelve sections. Blue squills, stars, and meadowlarks open the book; St. Louis sunsets, Cuban gardens, and Santa Barbara springs follow. Later sections hold war poems, including the famed There Will Come Soft Rains, and quiet songs of loss.

Teasdale writes in short, clear lines, with images of sea, night, and season. Love here is tender and often fleeting, yet never bitter. The book marks Teasdale at her mature best, where plain music carries deep feeling without show.
5960-little-sister-snow:
Frances Little sets her tale in Japan, in a quaint old garden under early spring sun. Light loosens a tiny rivulet from winter's grip and speeds it toward a miniature lake where goldfish dart. Into this scene comes Yuki Chan, a child who takes a stray petal blown into her face as a challenge.

The illustrations promise prayer, paint and brush, tea service, and lonely hours, with old people and a father's summons in the background. Little writes for readers who enjoy a gentle, picture-filled story. The child's small acts of courage and devotion carry a tale of life in a Japanese household.
6044-quill-s-window:
George Barr McCutcheon opens Quill's Window on a hot August day, as a young man and an old one sit in willow shade beside a wide, still river. Sun glare fails to pierce their shelter, while out on the slow river it beats down and raises a pale vapor that dazzles the eye.

Chapters promise a forbidden rock, a story the old man told, Courtney Thane, Dowd's tavern, trespass, and a face at the window. Rosabel appears, shadows gather, and a disappearance, a thrower of stones, and a message with its answer follow. McCutcheon builds a riverside mystery around an old trail and a window.
693-the-autobiography-of-a-quack-and-the:
S. Weir Mitchell, a noted American doctor, paired two tales that first ran unsigned in the Atlantic Monthly. The first is the boastful memoir of a quack, a fake healer who lives by tricks, fine talk, and the trust of the sick. The second is the case notes of George Dedlow, a soldier who wakes after battle to find his limbs gone.

Mitchell recast the quack tale at length and notes that the Dedlow case was taken by many readers as real, with money raised for the sufferer. The pair shows both sides of his art: satire on medical fraud, and a sober study of pain and loss after war. Together they mark an early step in American medical fiction.
7774-the-journal-of-arthur-stirling-the-:
Upton Sinclair edits and condenses The Journal of Arthur Stirling, subtitled The Valley of the Shadow, with an introductory sketch. Stirling, known to barely a dozen people in a huge city, was Sinclair's close friend, a self-taught man who worked many hard jobs by day and studied by night.

He taught himself five languages, knew more great poetry by heart than any man of letters Sinclair knew, and wrote a blank-verse tragedy called The Captive. The journal records a life of fierce artistic devotion, poverty, and hope, and stands as a portrait of talent unnoticed by the world.
7953-behind-the-bungalow:
Writing as Eha, Edward Hamilton Aitken gathered these papers from the Times of India into a book first published for readers of the Bombay Presidency. Illustrated by F. C. Macrae and here in its sixth edition of 1897, it describes life behind an Anglo-Indian bungalow. The servants, or nowkers, run the household, from the bearer who brings tea and slippers to the many hands behind every daily task. The Indian servant, Aitken notes, shows much the same traits wherever he is found.

The sketches are humorous and affectionate, though written from the employer's side of the veranda. They preserve a vivid picture of colonial domestic life: its routines, misunderstandings, and small diplomacies. Modern readers will enjoy the wit while also seeing, clearly, the unequal world that made such households possible.
8084-hunting-with-the-bow-arrow:
Saxton Pope wrote this book on hunting with the bow and arrow, with forty-eight illustrations, dedicating it to Robin Hood, a spirit that dwells in the heart of every youth. Its chapters begin with the story of Ishi, the last Yana Indian, his bow and arrow, and his methods of hunting. Then turn to archery in general: how to make a bow and arrow, equipment, how to shoot, and the principles of hunting. Later chapters cover raccoon, deer, bear, mountain lions, grizzly, and Alaskan adventures.

Pope, a physician and friend of Ishi, helped revive traditional archery in America, and his book mixes anthropology with practical instruction. It teaches the craft from the ground up, with respect for the Native teacher at its centre. For archers and readers of outdoor literature, it remains a foundational and humane classic.
8413-the-bishop-s-shadow:
I. T. Thurston wrote The Bishop's Shadow for young readers, with illustrations by M. Eckerson. Contents open with a lost pocketbook, Nan's new home, an accident, and Tode meeting the bishop, and the epigraph speaks of shadows: our influence may fall where we can never be. The bishop's shadow, in other words, is the good a life casts beyond itself.

Thurston, author of Boys of the Central and A Genuine Lady, writes in the wholesome children's tradition of the day, with plucky young people and moral lessons worn lightly. Readers of old-fashioned juvenile fiction will find a gentle, earnest story, where small kindnesses and accidents shape lives. It is a period piece, best read as such.
849-the-idle-thoughts-of-an-idle-fellow:
Jerome K. Jerome wrote these essays by an idle fellow, who defends idleness as a fine art. He muses on being idle, on love, on cats and dogs, and on the vanity of busy folk, in prose that is witty, confessional, and warm. The dedication, to a friend of prosperous and evil days, sets the joking tone.

Jerome's idle fellow is no fool: he watches human nature with a sharp eye and a kind heart. The essays, short and urbane, made Jerome famous before Three Men in a Boat. The book charms readers who enjoy light philosophy, where a lazy afternoon yields more truth than a week of hustle.
8902-the-flight-of-the-shadow:
George MacDonald opens The Flight of the Shadow with Mrs Day beginning the story, followed by Miss Martha Moon, an uncle, his room, and the narrator's first secret. Losing herself, a mirror, Thanatos and Zoe, a garden, and once more a secret carry the early chapters, before the mole burrows, a letter arrives, and old love meets new. Mother and uncle, the time between, fault and no fault, a summons, and John seeing something raise the tension.

John taken ill, a strange visit, and a foiled attempt continue the mystery, as a shadow, literal and moral, pursues the family. MacDonald blends domestic realism with fairy-tale dread, in the manner of his Scottish romances. Readers who know MacDonald from children's books will find a darker, adult novel here, concerned with conscience, inheritance, and the secrets that shape a household across generations.
9080-the-children-s-own-longfellow:
This illustrated gift book gathers poems by Henry Wadsworth Longfellow chosen for young readers. It holds favorites that American children long learned by heart. The Wreck of the Hesperus leads the set. The Village Blacksmith and Paul Revere's Ride follow, with parts of Evangeline and The Song of Hiawatha.

The picks favor clear stories, strong rhythms, and scenes a child can picture, from a ship in a storm to a smith at his forge. Longfellow's fame as America's household poet rests in part on just such verse. The book still works as a first meeting with a poet whose lines once rang in schoolrooms across the land.
9155-heather-and-snow:
George MacDonald wrote this Scots novel of heather hills, snow, and strong-willed folk. Its people include David and his daughter, Kirsty, Francis Gordon, and Phemy Craig. A runaway race opens the tale, and love, pride, and kinship drive it on through storms, abductions, and a race with death.

MacDonald sets the story in a Scotland of crofts, kirks, and winter roads, with Scots speech flavoring the talk. Kirsty's grit and heart anchor the plot. Readers who love Victorian tales of character and place will find here a warm, rugged story.
9786-love-s-shadow:
Ada Leverson wrote Love's Shadow in 1908, the first book of her Little Ottleys series. Edith and Bruce Ottley, young and pretty, live in a very new, very small, very white flat in Knightsbridge. Bruce begs Edith not to make him late at the office, while Edith, cheerful and intelligent, hides a subtler mind. A Shakespeare verse on love like a shadow fronts the book.

The novel follows the Ottleys' marriage through letters, mornings, and social calls, with wit as its chief weapon. Leverson writes with light, ironic grace, fond of her foolish, charming folk. A reader gets a witty Edwardian comedy of marriage, and the start of a beloved comic series.
aaron-trow:
Anthony Trollope opens with a warning about Bermuda: he will never regard those islets as the Fortunate Islands of the ancients. Getting in or out, he writes, tries any sailor's patience, and Caliban fits the place better than Ariel. On one of those islands lives a quiet clerk, Caleb Morton, and his wife, in a lonely house.

Aaron Trow, an escaped convict from the hulks, breaks into that house by night, and the tale tightens into a hunt across the island's cedar groves and inlets. Trollope, best known for cathedral towns and drawing rooms, here writes a grim, compact story of terror and pursuit. It appeared in his Tales of All Countries of 1864.
and-even-now:
Max Beerbohm gathered essays written over ten years and dated each one, as his note from Rapallo in 1920 explains. The contents run from A Relic of 1918 to pieces on hosts and guests, servants, going out for a walk, and laughter. An old portmanteau found in a cupboard opens the first essay.

Beerbohm writes on books within books, a clergyman, speaking French, and a house among the pines, always with the same light, exact prose and gentle irony. The war years shadow several pieces without darkening their poise. The book shows the essayist in maturity, amused by the world and quietly sad at its changes.
at-the-foot-of-the-rainbow:
Gene Stratton-Porter set At the Foot of the Rainbow along Indiana's Wabash River, among trappers, fishermen, and the birds of the Limberlost country she made famous. The contents promise rat-catchers, coon hunts, kingfishers, and black bass, mixed with the Malone family's troubles. Dannie Micrander and Jimmy Malone, boyhood friends, stand at the center.

Jimmy drinks, neglects his wife Mary, and drifts toward ruin while Dannie quietly loves Mary and holds to his renunciation. Fishing and trapping scenes carry the nature writing Stratton-Porter readers expected, exact about seasons and animal habits. The closing chapters bring confession, sacrifice, and the pot of gold the title promises, in her warm moral style.
blacky-the-crow:
Thornton W. Burgess opens Blacky the Crow with a warning about his hero's eyes. Blacky is forever spying out things never meant for his sharp eyes. In this he resembles his cousin Sammy Jay, Burgess writes. Winter locks up the Big River and the Smiling Pool, and food is scarce.

Blacky flies to a lonesome corner of the Green Forest where Redtail the Hawk once nested. In the old nest he finds eggs that are not Redtail's, and a mystery of the duck family begins. Ducky the Gadwall and his mate have trusted the empty nest. Blacky's discovery sets hunters, crows, and conscience at odds. Burgess tells the tale for young children, in short chapters with a naturalist's accuracy. Peter Rabbit and Happy Jack Squirrel comment from the sidelines, as his readers expected.
castle-craneycrow:
George Barr McCutcheon's Castle Craneycrow, printed at New York in 1902, opens with the taking of Turk. Philip Quentin, a rich young American, had caught the little burglar in his rooms at night. Instead of the police, he fed him supper and hired him. Turk — Turkington, or James — has served him faithfully for seven years.

Quentin travels to Florence, where Dorothy Garrison, an American heiress, is promised to an Italian prince. Quentin loves her, and the prince's mountain stronghold, Castle Craneycrow, gives the romance its Gothic machinery. An abduction, a siege of suitors, and Turk's underworld talents drive the plot. McCutcheon followed Graustark with this Italian companion piece, trading his invented kingdom for a real duchy's intrigues. The tone is lighter than the peril: a comedy of love against a castle wall, with a burglar as best man.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cracow:
A diocesan entry presents Cracow, the prince-bishopric covering western Galicia, bordering Russian Poland, Prussia, and Hungary. Already in existence by the year 1000, its founding is disputed: some argue for King Mieceslaw I in 984, while most place it at 1000 or just before.

Five lists of bishops survive, the oldest from about 1266, though names before Bishop Aaron are unreliable after Bohemian invaders destroyed records in 1039. Three bishops are publicly venerated, above all St. Stanislaus, martyred by King Boleslaw and canonized in 1253. The entry closes with the diocese in music history, as birthplace of the violin makers Amati, Guarneri, and Stradivari.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-friedrich-wil:
Friedrich Wilhelm Schadow, a Berlin painter born in 1789, led the Düsseldorf Academy to fame in the nineteenth century. Son of the sculptor Johann Gottfried Schadow, he joined the circle around Overbeck at Rome and there became a Catholic. He taught at Berlin from 1819, then moved to Düsseldorf in 1826 as academy director, with many pupils following him.

Schadow prized realism, color, and sober restraint, grounded in strict drawing from plaster casts before nature. He favored oil painting and modest subjects over grand frescoes: devotional scenes, portraits, landscapes, and genre pieces. His Wise and Foolish Virgins, his Four Evangelists, and his Paradise, Purgatory, and Hell show a graceful talent that valued poetic thought above bold form.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-glasgow:
Glasgow is an archdiocese in the southwest of Scotland, covering Lanark, Dumbarton, and Renfrew, part of Ayrshire, Baldernock in Stirlingshire, and the Cumbrae Isles. Saint Kentigern, or Mungo, founded the see between 540 and 560 and died in 601. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a see restored under Saint David after centuries without regular succession.

Kentigern built a religious community on the Welsh model to preserve the faith among the surrounding Christians. The restored see's first bishop, John Eochy, held it from 1115 to 1147. Twenty-three successors followed in actual possession until 1560, when Parliament abolished the Catholic faith. Its bishops served as chancellors, treasurers, and regents, and William Turnbull won the charter for the University of Glasgow in 1450.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jakob-benignu:
Physician and anatomist Jakob Benignus Winslow was born at Odense, Denmark, on 27 April 1669. He died at Paris on 3 April 1760. He finished high school at Odense in 1687. He then attended Copenhagen university, studying philosophy and theology. Later he chose medicine and earned a bachelor's degree in 1694. On a royal scholarship he went abroad for training in 1697. He reached Paris in spring 1698.

There he met the Catholic religion. A thorough study of controverted questions, begun to strengthen his Lutheran faith, brought him into the Church instead. Bossuet himself received his profession of faith on 8 October 1699. Conversion made return to Denmark impossible. Despite money troubles, he continued medical studies under Duverney. In autumn 1704 he received his licentiate degree free of charge. The entry presents a convert anatomist of Paris.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-barrow:
John Barrow was a Lancashire priest of notable courage who served the Claughton mission for forty-five years. Born at Westby-in-the-Fylde in 1735 to stout Catholic yeomen, he spent seven years studying at the English College in Rome. Pressed into service at Portsmouth, he spent five years in the navy. He then deserted at Dunkirk and talked his way past a court-martial by pretending to know only Italian.

Ordained at Douai in 1766, he rode to Claughton that July and stayed until his death in 1811. Master of French and Italian, writer of elegant Latin and forceful English, he enlarged the parish church. He improved roads as township overseer, reinvested clergy funds wisely, and negotiated the land for Ushaw College. Though he sometimes slighted his own bishop's wishes, he demanded obedience to Church authority from everyone else, and Rome praised his loyalty and zeal.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-matthew-of-cr:
A scholar, preacher, and envoy, Matthew of Cracow was born about 1335 and died at Pisa in 1410. The old tale of noble Pomeranian blood is now discredited; his father was likely a notary at Cracow. He took degrees at Prague, served as dean there, and by 1387 appears as a professor of theology and city preacher. In 1395 he moved to Heidelberg, became rector a year later, and counselled the ruler Ruprecht II.

Ruprecht III's rise as King of Rome in 1400 opened a statesman's career. It brought embassies and court missions, including a plea at Rome in 1403 and greetings to Innocent VII in 1404. Named Bishop of Worms that year, he kept teaching at Heidelberg and declined a cardinal's hat. His writings span Bible commentaries, sermons, and works on confession, conscience, the Eucharist, and the Mass.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-matthew-of-ja:
Matthew of Janow, a Bohemian church writer of the fourteenth century, died at Prague in 1394. Son of the knight Wenzel of Janow, he studied at Prague and Paris, earning the title Parisian Master after nine years abroad. In 1381 he became canon and confessor at Prague Cathedral, posts he held for life, and he won note less for preaching than for zeal in the confessional.

Between 1388 and 1392 he gathered his treatises as the Regulae Veteris et Novi Testamenti, a work never printed whole and nowhere surviving complete. Parts were wrongly printed among Hus's writings. Blaming the Papal Schism and abuses around exemptions, relics, and images, he urged daily Communion for lay folk. He also urged the removal of images from churches, views the Prague synod of 1389 rejected. He later retracted, and the entry insists he was no forerunner of Hus.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-moscow:
Moscow, Russian Moskva, was Russia's ancient capital and chief city of its province. It stands near the centre of European Russia on both banks of the river that gives it its name. Fourth capital after Novgorod, Kiev and Vladimir, it housed the tsars from 1340 until Peter the Great moved the court in 1711. Poets call it Bielokamennaya, the White-Walled.

Its population reached 1,335,104 by 1907, making it Russia's greatest commercial and industrial city. It held 440 churches, 24 convents, over 500 schools including the university, some 502 charitable establishments and 23 cemeteries. The entry divides the city grown around the Kremlin into five concentric parts. It follows its churches, monasteries, Catholic parishes and history from foundation to modern times.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-our-lady-of-t:
Our Lady of the Snow is a feast kept on 5 August to mark the dedication of Santa Maria Maggiore on Rome's Esquiline Hill. Pope Liberius built the first church there between 352 and 366, and it bore his name, Basilica Liberii. Pope Sixtus III restored it between 432 and 440 and dedicated it to Our Lady, and from the seventh century it also bore the name Mary at the Manger.

The name of the snow, and the legend behind it, came a few hundred years later. The tale tells how the childless patrician John and his wife vowed their wealth to Our Lady. They prayed to learn how to spend it, and woke on 5 August to snow on the Esquiline summit. Following a vision of the same night, they built a basilica on the snow-covered spot. No mention of the marvel appears until centuries later, not even in Sixtus's own dedication lines.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-richard-brist:
Richard Bristow was born at Worcester in 1538 and died at Harrow-on-the-Hill in 1581. Oxford took him in 1555, likely to Exeter College, though Wood doubts the college link. He took his bachelor's degree in 1559 and proceeded Master of Arts at Christ Church in 1562. Exceptionally brilliant and eloquent, he was esteemed as an orator so highly that, with Edmund Campion, he was chosen to dispute publicly before Queen Elizabeth in 1566.

Soon after, having turned to theology and won a wide name for learning, he became a Fellow of Exeter College in 1567 through Sir William Petre, founder of several fellowships there. His ability would probably have won him further promotion, but his religious opinions changed, as an argument with the Regius Professor already showed. The entry follows a scholar whose changing opinions checked a rising Oxford career.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rose-window:
A rose window is a round window whose mullions and tracery spread out from the centre, filled with stained glass. The name comes from its fancied resemblance to a rose and its petals. It is one of the most beautiful features of medieval architecture, especially French Gothic. Its origin lies in the Roman oculus, which became a window in the Romanesque period.

By the mid-thirteenth century it had reached its greatest size, the entire width of the nave. Its splendour lasted in France until later fourteenth- and fifteenth-century misfortunes halted large church building. The finest examples stand in the Ile de France and nearby Picardy and Champagne, including Mantes about 1200 and Notre Dame of Paris about 1220. Later steps put the rose under a pointed arch, as at Reims in 1230, then inscribed it in a square, as in the Paris transepts of 1257.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-school-of-dur:
Durrow, Irish Dairmagh, Plain of the Oaks, lies delightfully in King's County a few miles from Tullamore. Columba, who loved building near oak groves for their beauty and to strip them of druidic associations, found here, as at Derry, a site after his heart. His entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia follows a monastery through exile and succession quarrels.

Aedh, son of Brendan, lord of the soil, freely gave the site in 553, and Columba founded his monastery, ruling it with more or less steady care until 563. That year, whether in penance or, as Adamnan says, by choice for Christ's sake, he sailed into Scottish exile. He named Cormac Ua Liathain to succeed him, but tribal jealousies between north and south drove Cormac out, leaving Columba's cousin Laisren in charge.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-margaret-c:
Margaret Clitherow, Pearl of York, was pressed to death for harbouring priests and refusing to plead. Born about 1556 to Thomas Middleton, York's sheriff in 1564 and 1565 and a wax-chandler, she married John Clitherow, a wealthy butcher and city chamberlain, at St. Martin's, Coney Street, on 8 July 1571. They lived in the Shambles. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates her death to 25 March 1586.

Converted about three years later, she grew fervent, risking life by harbouring and maintaining priests. She endured frequent imprisonment, sometimes for two years, yet never daunted. Though her husband was of the Established Church, his brother was a priest. Margaret kept two hiding chambers, one adjoining her house and one elsewhere in the city, with Mass celebrated continually through persecution's thickest years. Some of her priests died martyrs, and Margaret, longing for the same grace, made secret night pilgrimages to York Tyburn.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-stanislaus:
Stanislaus of Cracow, bishop and martyr, is patron of Poland and its ancient capital. Born at Szczepanów on 26 July 1030 to the pious nobles Belislaus and Bogna, he studied at Gniezno and perhaps Paris. After his parents died he gave his ample inheritance to the poor. Bishop Lambert Zula ordained him, made him pastor, canon, cathedral preacher, and vicar-general.

On Lambert's death he was elected bishop, accepting only on Pope Alexander II's explicit command. He worked with energy for reform, but clashed with King Boleslaus II, whom he excommunicated for cruelty and injustice. The king struck him down, tradition says at Mass, on 8 May 1079. No contemporary life survives, and his canonisation life mixes legend with history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-stanislawow:
Stanislawów, a diocese of the Greek-Ruthenian rite in Galicia, served nearly a million faithful under Austria. Its establishment was decided in May 1850 but took effect only with the brief De universo dominico grege of 26 March 1885 and imperial decrees that December. Suffragan of Lwów, it covered most of south-eastern Galicia and all Bukovina as far as Halicz.

It counted twenty-one deaneries and sixty-three chapels. It held 433 churches with resident priests and 298 without. Its clergy numbered 579 secular and thirteen regular priests. It also held four Reformed Basilian monasteries, two Basilian convents, and ten convents of the Servants of the Blessed Virgin. Greek-Ruthenian Catholics numbered 920,000 of a population of 1,387,930, beside Armenians and Latins. A seminary opened in 1907, after clergy trained at Lwów and Vienna. Its town was founded by Stanislav Potocki, dead in 1683.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tarnow:
Tarnow is a diocese of western Galicia in Austria. Posen, founded in 968 by Duke Miecyslaw, stood alone in Poland until 1100. That year Otto III and Duke Boleslaw founded Gnesen and Cracow, to which western Galicia then belonged. In the First Partition of 1772 that land fell to Austria. It was cut from foreign Cracow and run from Tarnow by vicar-general Johann von Duval. He became first bishop when the see was erected in 1783.

After the Third Partition of 1795 brought Cracow to Austria too, the see was split. On the second bishop's death in 1801 it was divided between Cracow and Przemysl. Vienna's peace of 1809 handed western Galicia to the Duchy of Warsaw, and Tarnow fell under Lemberg. The Congress of Vienna restored Galicia to Austria. Francis then gave Tarnow a new bishop in 1822, Gregorius Thomas Ziegler, who settled at Tarnow in 1826 after stops at Tyniec and Bochnia.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-universit:
Poland's university at Cracow, planned by Casimir the Great, is traced here from first documents to full faculties. Evidence for the scheme dates from 1362, Urban V favoured it, and Casimir chartered the university on 12 May 1364, modelled on Padua and Bologna, with law and Roman law first. Papal approval of 1 September 1364 excluded theology.

Jagiello and Hedwig of Anjou refounded the school. Boniface IX consented on 11 February 1397, and Jagiello signed a new charter on 26 July 1400, now with all four faculties on the Paris pattern. Bishop Peter Wysz, first chancellor, gave the opening lecture. Bohemian, German, and Polish professors, trained mostly at Prague, taught 205 students in year one, rising to 500.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-edward-am:
Edward Ambrose Barlow, alias Radcliffe and Brereton, was a priest and martyr born at Barlow Hall in 1585, who died on 10 September 1641. Fourth son of Sir Alexander Barlow of Barlow Hall near Manchester and Mary Brereton of Handforth Hall, he was baptized at Didsbury Church on 30 November 1585. The register entry may still be seen. Schooled at the Benedictine monastery of St Gregory, Douai, he entered the English College at Valladolid in 1610.

He returned to Douai, where his elder brother William Rudesind was a professed monk, was professed himself in 1616, and ordained in 1617. Sent to England, he laboured in south Lancashire with apostolic zeal, living chiefly at Wardley Hall and Morley's Hall. Arrested in 1641, he was condemned for his priesthood and suffered at Lancaster, steadfast to the end.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-john-fing: F. M. Rudge's Catholic Encyclopedia entry records John Finglow, an English martyr born at Barnby near Howden in Yorkshire. Ordained priest at the English College, Reims, on 25 March 1581, he was sent on the English mission the following month and laboured in the north. Seized and held in Ousebridge Kidcote at York, he was tried as a Catholic priest for reconciling subjects to the old faith, then hanged, drawn and quartered on 8 August 1586.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-peter-sno: John Wainewright's Catholic Encyclopedia entry traces Peter Snow, an English martyr born at or near Ripon. He arrived at the English College, Reims, in April 1589, took tonsure and minor orders in 1590, and was ordained deacon and priest at Soissons in March 1591. He left for England that May. Arrested about 1 May 1598 on his way to York with Ralph Grimston of Nidd, Snow was condemned for treason as a priest and suffered at York on 15 June 1598.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-william-b:
William Barrow, alias Waring or Harcourt, was an English Jesuit executed at Tyburn in June 1679. Born in Lancashire in 1609, he studied at St-Omer, entered the Society at Watten in 1632, and worked the London district for thirty-five years, becoming its superior early in 1678.

That May he was arrested and sent to Newgate on charges linked to the alleged Popish Plot. His trial with fellow Jesuits Thomas Whitbread, John Fenwick, John Gavan, and Anthony Turner became infamous. Chief Justice Scroggs ruled that the accusers' recent royal pardons barred any mention of their past misdeeds, and that no Catholic witness could be believed. Though the prisoners exposed wholesale perjury by Oates, Bedloe, and Dugdale, they were condemned for high treason and suffered together at Tyburn.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-widow:
Widow is treated here through canonical prescriptions, above all in the Old Testament, where remarriage law dominates. The high priest might not marry a widow, while other priests might marry a fellow priest's widow but not a layman's.

Outside those rules no Old Testament law restricted a widow's remarriage. Support for widows was commended to Israelite charity: they received gleanings of cornfields, olive trees. Vineyards, a share in the third year's tithe, and invitations to feast with the nearest householder at the three principal solemnities. In Maccabean times money and provisions were kept in Jerusalem's Temple for widows' subsistence, and battle spoils were shared with them. For their protection the law forbade taking a widow's garment in pawn, and Job counts seizing a widow's ox for a pledge a wicked act.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-rudes:
William Rudesind Barlow was an English Benedictine scholar counted the chief schoolman of his age. His birth date is uncertain; he died at Douai on 19 September 1656. Third son of Sir Alexander Barlow of Barlow Hall, he was schooled with his younger brother, the martyr Edward Barlow, at Douai. Wishing to become a Benedictine, he professed with the Spanish congregation at Cella Nueva in Galicia in 1605 and took his doctorate at Salamanca.

Ordained in 1608, Barlow became prior of Saint Gregory's, Douai, in 1614 and taught theology at Saint Vaast's for forty years, shaping nearly all the bishops, abbots, and teachers of those parts. Weldon calls him first among scholastic divines and casuists, inferior to none in canon law. He refused abbacies and bishoprics, led the English Congregation as president-general from 1621 to 1629, and left almost no writings, his papers destroyed by an enemy after his death.
crome-yellow:
Aldous Huxley's first novel, Crome Yellow, opens on a slow train through Bole, Tritton, and Spavin Delawarr, stations Denis Stone knows by heart. Denis, a young poet, travels to Crome, the country house of Henry Wimbush, for a weekend of artists and talkers. He piles his chattels neatly in the corner, in the futile way the narrator mocks at once.

The house party includes the deaf Anne and the painter Gombauld. The historian host reads his county history aloud. Prophets of the future like Mr Scogan compare Caesars to queen bees raised by special food. Huxley's satire of Bloomsbury and peacock talk made his name in 1921. Denis's failed romance keeps the wit humane.
dark-hollow:
Anna Katharine Green's Dark Hollow, published by Dodd, Mead in New York in 1914, begins with a gate standing ajar. Judge Ostrander's house in Shelby has opened its doors to no outsider for over a dozen years. A group of neighbours gathers, eager and hesitating, before the fence. The woman in purple has been seen at the gate.

Books one to three unwind the judge's buried secret: a man killed years ago, a servant named Bela, and a wife who vanished. Deborah Scranton, a widow of courage, forces the gates from outside. Courtroom scenes, a bit of steel, and unwelcome truths prepare the vigil at Tempest Lodge. Green, a founder of the detective novel, builds her mystery on character and conscience. The curtain lifts at last on Dark Hollow itself, in a sunset of expiation.
doe-osti-3021347-collaborative-fundament: Zeolite catalysts getting thirsty got their DOE water study, and this text watches the synthesis sip. The pages detail the behavior results. The chemists get their data. The study was collaborative. The sip was synthesis. The thirsty were zeolite. The water was study.
doe-osti-3024210-pumped-thermal-energy-s: Pumped thermal got particle-storaged, and this DOE text uses fluid bed exchangers. The pages detail the maximum findings. The energy folks get their data. The efficiency was power. The data were energy. The bed were fluid. The exchanger was heat.
doe-osti-3624639-a-multiomics-mass-spect: Strains got multiomics-optimized, and this DOE abstract covers mass spectrometry workflows. The pages detail the workflow findings. The biologists get their data. The CRADA was 726. The data were biologist. The 726 were CRADA. The optimization were strain. The abstract were findings.
doe-osti-3912522-frequency-extraction-fr: Accelerator beams wobble at characteristic frequencies — reading them reveals the machine's health. Yongjun Li's work extracts frequencies from invariant flows, the orderly patterns hidden in beam motion. The technique gives operators a sharper diagnostic for tuning their machines.
fern-s-hollow: Fern's Hollow, by Hesba Stretton. The hollow's tale. This book preserves that children's story. The paper lived through the years. Coming generations can find it. Its place in history is secure. Kept for study. The archive keeps the paper open to all who seek it.
flame-and-shadow:
Sara Teasdale's Flame and Shadow, published after Love Songs made her famous, groups its lyrics in five numbered sections. Early poems like Blue Squills, Stars, and I Have Loved Hours at Sea set her themes: nature watched closely, love gained and lost, and time passing. A French motto about receiving flame or shadow opens the book.

Later sections move through places, day and night, pain, and spring torrents, with titles such as In a Hospital, The Broken Field, and If I Must Go. Teasdale's diction stays plain while her images sharpen, a leaf or a lizard carrying whole moods. The collection won admirers for its music and restraint, and it shows her art at full maturity.
from-a-college-window:
Arthur Christopher Benson published From a College Window in 1906, gathering essays from the Cornhill Magazine. Benson, a fellow of Magdalene College at Cambridge, begins with the point of view. Sincerity, he argues, gives any work of art its value. Charm cannot be manufactured, but an honest outlook can be chosen.

Eighteen papers follow on growing older, books, conversation, and sociability. Beauty, art, egotism, and education each receive a quiet hearing. Ambition and the simple life are weighed against each other. Games, spiritualism, habits, and religion close the set. Benson writes from his window in a level, confiding voice. The essays made him the best-loved English essayist of his generation, a don thinking aloud for readers who wanted reflection without system.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_chile_Ex:
On September 15, 1970, President Richard Nixon met in the Oval Office for twenty minutes with his advisers.
